chunks: "First I'd ask whether I need it, because every doubling costs efficiency and EMI. Assuming I do, I attack the limiters. Switching loss: make the transitions shorter.

A stronger gate driver and a lower gate resistor shorten the Miller plateau: with a 5 volt drive, a 10 ohm resistor gives about 25 nanoseconds for a 5 nanocoulomb gate-drain charge; 47 ohms gives 117.
Pick a MOSFET with a better figure of merit, lower gate charge times on-resistance, lower output capacitance.
Reduce the parasitic inductance in the power loop and the gate loop with layout, so I can run fast edges without ringing.
Use synchronous rectification so the freewheel diode's reverse recovery doesn't add loss. Go to GaN or SiC if I need hundreds of kilohertz to megahertz.
Fixed times: use a driver with short, matched propagation delay and adaptive or smaller dead time, shorten the current-sense blanking with good layout.
A cheaper trick for a motor: make the load see a higher frequency without switching the devices faster.
A three-level unipolar H-bridge doubles the effective ripple frequency, and interleaved phases multiply it, so the ripple drops without more loss.
Then support it: a timer with enough resolution, thermal design, and EMI measures like slew-rate control, filters and layout."
